label: Recall, spacing and mixing
summary: Making learning last: asking learners to bring ideas back from memory, coming back to them after a gap, and mixing kinds of problems once each is learned.

items.text: Once they have worked through something, ask them to bring it back from memory without looking, rather than showing it again.
items.attribution: Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249-255. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x Yang, C., Luo, L., Vadillo, M. A., Yu, R., & Shanks, D. R. (2021). Testing (quizzing) boosts classroom learning: A systematic and meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin, 147(4), 399-435. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000309

items.text: Have them write or say the answer themselves rather than pick from options: recalling helps more than recognizing.
items.attribution: Rowland, C. A. (2014). The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect. Psychological Bulletin, 140(6), 1432-1463. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037559

items.text: After they try to recall, say what was right and what was missing: practice with correction works better than practice alone.
items.attribution: Yang, C., Luo, L., Vadillo, M. A., Yu, R., & Shanks, D. R. (2021). Testing (quizzing) boosts classroom learning: A systematic and meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin, 147(4), 399-435. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000309 Butler, A. C., & Roediger, H. L. (2008). Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing. Memory & Cognition, 36(3), 604-616. https://doi.org/10.3758/MC.36.3.604

items.text: When they are stuck, ask what they remember about it before you re-explain, and say a wrong guess is fine: even a failed attempt helps what they learn next to stick.
items.attribution: Kornell, N., Hays, M. J., & Bjork, R. A. (2009). Unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhance subsequent learning. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 35(4), 989-998. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0015729 Pan, S. C., & Carpenter, S. K. (2023). Prequestioning and pretesting effects: A review of empirical research, theoretical perspectives, and implications for educational practice. Educational Psychology Review, 35(4), 97. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09814-5

items.text: Come back to an idea after other work, later in the conversation or in a later session, and ask for it again rather than repeating it straight away.
items.source: Cepeda et al. 2006; Carpenter et al. 2022
items.attribution: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354-380. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354 Carpenter, S. K., Pan, S. C., & Butler, A. C. (2022). The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice. Nature Reviews Psychology, 1(9), 496-511. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-022-00089-1

items.text: Don't stop at the first correct recall: ask again a few times, and return to it on a later day.
items.attribution: Rawson, K. A., & Dunlosky, J. (2011). Optimizing schedules of retrieval practice for durable and efficient learning: How much is enough? Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 140(3), 283-302. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0023956

items.text: Once they can do each kind of problem, mix in an earlier kind so they must decide which method applies, rather than repeating the last one.
items.about: math mathematics maths algebra equation fraction decimal geometry arithmetic ratio percent calculus statistics
items.attribution: Rohrer, D., Dedrick, R. F., Hartwig, M. K., & Cheung, C.-N. (2020). A randomized controlled trial of interleaved mathematics practice. Journal of Educational Psychology, 112(1), 40-52. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000367 Rohrer, D., & Taylor, K. (2007). The shuffling of mathematics problems improves learning. Instructional Science, 35(6), 481-498. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9015-8

items.text: If two kinds of problem get confused, mix them on purpose and ask which is which before solving. Don't do this with word lists or a text: there it hasn't been shown to help.
items.attribution: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin, 145(11), 1029-1052. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209

cite: VIABLE Lab (2026). Recall, spacing and mixing: guidance from research. The wording is VIABLE Lab's; each piece names the studies it draws on.

evidence.original: Among the best replicated findings in the science of learning. Repeated recall beat restudy on delayed tests, even though restudy raised confidence (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006, students reading prose). Recall gives more than recognition (Rowland, 2014); classroom quizzing g = 0.499 across 222 studies and 48,478 students, moderated by corrective feedback among other things (Yang et al., 2021). A systematic review of 50 classroom experiments found mostly medium or large benefits, only 6% in non-WEIRD countries (Agarwal et al., 2021). Trying before studying helps even when the attempt fails, in lab experiments with the answer shown after; size varies by procedure (Kornell et al., 2009; Richland et al., 2009; Pan & Carpenter, 2023). Spacing: 317 experiments (Cepeda et al., 2006); the best gap grows with how long the learning must last (Cepeda et al., 2008). A major review rates practice testing and spacing high, interleaving moderate (Dunlosky et al., 2013). Relearning: three correct recalls, then three spaced sessions (Rawson & Dunlosky, 2011). Interleaving in math: college students (Rohrer & Taylor, 2007); grade 7, d = 0.42 and 0.79 (Rohrer et al., 2015); 54 grade 7 classes, 61% against 38%, d = 0.83 (Rohrer et al., 2020). Across materials g = 0.42, math 0.34, nothing clear for expository text, and blocking is better for words (Brunmair & Richter, 2019).
evidence.integration: Not yet compared with and without it in this harness.
evidence.unknown: Few of these studies involve a tutor in conversation, and none an AI. Spacing needs a learner to come back: within one chat the gaps are short, and the Harness keeps no memory across sessions unless a host passes history. How many recall questions a learner will accept from a tutor before it feels like a quiz is not known. Interleaving's classroom evidence is almost all math.

risk_notes: Its text goes to a model as guidance. Nothing runs and nothing about a learner goes anywhere. What the teacher set for how far to go comes first. Most of the research is about human tutors, so a piece can still misfit a learner or a moment.
